10316-roy-blakeley-s-adventures-in-camp:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh published this Boy Scout story in 1920, with Roy Blakeley as its cheerful narrator. Roy tells how his patrol got started, found a paper, and made for Temple Camp on the Hudson. The book belongs to a series that praised scout craft, loyalty, and fun.

Skinny, a younger boy, seeks a merit badge, learns to swim, and joins rows on Black Lake, while storms and strange campers test the troop. Camp-fire talks and a talk with Bert Winton round out the tale. Readers get a warm, funny scout adventure, told in Roy's own breezy voice.
10904-frank-merriwell-s-nobility-or-the-:
Burt L. Standish published Frank Merriwell's Nobility, or The Tragedy of the Ocean Tramp, in Tip Top Weekly on April 22, 1899. The story opens as the tramp steamer Eagle leaves New York for Liverpool, with Yale students on the pier waving hands, hats, and handkerchiefs. On deck stand Frank Merriwell, Bruce Browning, Jack Diamond, Harry Rattleton, and their tutor.

Frank's scheme for Europe drives the tale, with a tragedy aboard the ocean tramp to follow. Standish writes the clean, plucky adventure that made Merriwell a hero to American boys. Readers get a classic dime-novel voyage, full of school spirit and sea danger.
12729-the-high-school-boys-in-summer-cam:
H. Irving Hancock's High School Boys in Summer Camp, or The Dick Prescott Six Training for the Gridley Eleven, follows Gridley boys to camp. Chapters run from the man in the four-quart hat and Dick and some high finance through a human mystery of the woods. Dave Darrin angry, Dick grappling in the dark, danger on the hoof and a mad stampede follow.

Visitors for the feast, a woodland discovery, a new trap, a hard prowler, Tag Mosher, a fix, an ambulance case, a training bout, ten minutes of daring, a big storm and Mr. Page's kind of father follow. Hancock writes brisk schoolboy adventure, mixing football training with woodland mystery. The book is a lively summer tale for boy readers.
13510-knots-splices-and-rope-work-a-prac:
A. Hyatt Verrill gives complete, simple directions for useful and ornamental knots in this practical treatise, with chapters on splicing, pointing, seizing, and serving. Adapted for travellers, campers, yachtsmen, boy scouts, and all who handle ropes, the book carries more than one hundred and fifty illustrations in its full edition.

A catspaw is tied by taking twists with a bight in each hand and throwing them over a hook, while the Blackwall hitch, simpler still, is a loop or cuckold's neck. Pointing a rope means whipping, unlaying, and twisting yarns into left-handed nettles, then combing them out. Verrill writes for hands, not theory, so a reader can make a knot that holds.
1573-frank-s-campaign-or-the-farm-and-th:
Horatio Alger's Civil War tale for boys follows Frank, a Rossville farm boy whose town hall war meeting opens the book. When his father goes to war, Frank must run the farm, win a prize, and prove himself at home, while letters from the camp remind him of the larger struggle.

Alger's moral is plain: industry, honesty, and pluck win the day, on the farm as in the camp. The story moves between harvest work and soldier life with brisk, didactic charm. It is a typical Alger book, earnest and hopeful, written to stir young readers to duty and effort.
19522-tom-slade-at-temple-camp:
Percy K. Fitzhugh wrote this Boy Scout tale of Tom Slade at Temple Camp, published in Wisconsin in the late nineteen teens with scout approval. Roy's sacrifice, Indian scout signs, Pee-Wee and Mary Temple, and a mascot's first coup open a summer of tracks, trailing, and good turns.

A roadside joke about gasoline and soda shows the boys' easy humor, even when a trip goes wrong. The book teaches scout craft through story, and it keeps the series' faith that a good turn, done quietly, matters more than praise.
21306-dick-o-the-fens-a-tale-of-the-grea:
Dick Winthorpe, the squire's son, watches his father plan to drain the Lincolnshire fen and reclaim it as farmland. George Manville Fenn sets the tale in the great eastern swamp, where many locals live by the marsh and want it left alone. When digging starts, trouble follows: houses torched, horses and cows maimed, men shot, even murder.

A constable called in takes a dislike to Dick and his friend Tom Tallington. He tries to pin the crimes on them; at times even Dick's father half believes it. Broad Fenland dialect colours the talk. Fenland birds, boats, and weather fill the spaces between the crimes.
21723-songs-of-the-cattle-trail-and-cow-:
John A. Lomax gathered these cowboy songs and poems for a 1919 Macmillan volume, with a foreword by William Lyon Phelps. Lomax had spent years collecting American ballads, backed by a Harvard fellowship for the work. He had already published a well-known book of cowboy songs. Here he turns to the verse men sang and recited on the cattle trail and in cow camps.

The pieces range from trail songs to comic and tender poems by cowboy poets. Lomax prints them as working folklore, the art of men whose lives were spent on horseback. The book helps keep a fading oral world on the page. It remains a rich source for anyone studying the songs of the American West.
21757-the-hot-swamp:
Eight hundred years before Christ, a Phoenician sea captain named Arkal sails from a Greek port in this Ballantyne romance of old Albion. His ship carries one mast, a great square sail, and fifty oars, with a horse's head at the prow. Phoenician traders pushed past the Pillars of Hercules to the Tin Isles and beyond, seeking tin, amber, and gold.

Arkal's voyage toward Britain drives the tale, into seas and lands strange to his crew. Ballantyne sets his seafaring skills to work on the ancient world. The hot swamp of the title waits in the northern mists. It is a bold change of scene for him: his usual sea tale dressed in the oldest clothes of trade.
23436-aladdin-or-the-wonderful-lamp:
John McLoughlin printed this picture book version of Aladdin and the wonderful lamp, in rhymed verse with coloured plates. A wizard finds poor Aladdin, moves a stone from a cavern mouth, and sends the youth below ground through unknown realms to fetch a lamp from its niche.

Fruits that prove to be pearls, diamonds, and rubies dazzle Aladdin as he gathers treasure, and back home the lamp's genie brings food at a cry. The verse stays simple and musical, each scene paired with a picture for young readers. Children will love the magic, the cave, and the genie, while grown readers will enjoy this plain, old fashioned telling of a tale known the world over.
23645-the-motor-maids-at-sunrise-camp:
Katherine Stokes sent her Motor Maids to the mountains in this 1914 volume of the series, with Billie Campbell and her friends trading the road for a summer camp. Miss Helen Campbell chaperones, and a camp doctor keeps order. Chapters on rules, table manners, and a bog walk set the tone of cheerful, well-run outdoor life.

The story deepens when the girls befriend Phoebe, a ragged mountain girl who has lived all her life in a cabin, known no mother, and never had a friend. Gypsy cooks, a comedy of errors, a warning, and an attack keep the plot moving, but the camp's real work is kindness: giving Phoebe food, rest, and a place among companions.
24418-the-quantum-jump:
Robert Wicks wrote this story, with pictures by Llewellyn, for Amazing Science Fiction Stories in October 1958. Its blurb sets the puzzle: Captain Brandon explored space's far reaches and reported back. He finds it disquieting that the far reaches know more about home than he does. Brandon gazes at the Milky Way through his canopy, trailing like a bridal veil across black space.

Below his scout-ship stretch the red deserts of Sirius Three, lit by two ice moons. He thinks of the sun, 52 trillion miles off, a pinpoint lost in the Milky Way's dazzle, and Earth a speck in orbit, nine light years away. Thirteen years have passed on Earth since they left, for the trip took four years. They were shut in Astro One with five other men, above all Colonel Towers. Readers get a pioneer, far from home.
2712-a-drift-from-redwood-camp:
Bret Harte tells of a man all Redwood Camp knew as shiftless and worthless, who entered camp carrying his effects in a red handkerchief on a long handled shovel. In a community of strong men with sullen virtues and fascinating vices, no one expected better of him.

When the terrible inundation of 1856 comes, he lazily drifts out of camp on a plank, and the drift becomes his story. Harte turns a ne'er do well into an unlikely hero, with irony and pity. The tale shows his gift for finding worth in the last man anyone would pick.
28105-a-learned-dissertation-on-dumpling:
This Augustan Reprint Society volume pairs two anonymous eighteenth-century jests on food. The first, A Learned Dissertation on Dumpling from 1726, treats the humble dumpling with mock learned gravity. The second, Pudding and Dumpling Burnt to Pot from 1727, answers it as a complete key to the first piece.

Samuel L. Macey supplies an introduction for the 1970 reprint, issued by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at the University of California, Los Angeles. Together the two pamphlets show how Augustan writers used fake scholarship to mock fashion, taste, and learned pride. The humour still lands for readers who enjoy Swift's age.
30330-high-dragon-bump:
Don Thompson tells High Dragon Bump, illustrated by Paul Orban. A short tale, its tagline warns that if it took reduction or torch hair, the Cirissins wanted a bump, with hokum, thistle, and gluck. A young and beautiful girl with blond hair and smooth skin the colour of creamed sweet potatoes floats in the middle of a room. Wayne Brighton drifts into it, her few clothes concealing nothing.

Wayne, apprehension changing to confusion, asks whether she is going to reduce him. She answers that the word is seduce, mister, since they told her reduce too, but they do not talk good. She thinks she is supposed to seduce him so he will tell them something, and then they will let her go. Wayne says they want him to get them a high dragon bump, a thing he never heard of, and does not even know what it is.
30648-an-ocean-tramp:
William McFee writes An Ocean Tramp, published in Garden City, New York, in 1924 by Doubleday, Page, copyrighted in 1921. Books by McFee listed in the front matter include Aliens, Captain Macedoine's Daughter, Casuals of the Sea, and Port Said Miscellany. A Heine epigraph opens the book: she was lovable and he loved her, but he was not lovable and she did not love him.

A preface to the 1921 edition notes that by a justifiable artistic device, the letter writer, the ocean tramp himself, drowns at sea. Neither author nor publisher guaranteed the book as cold fact, and disillusion was not deemed necessary at first. McFee blends sea letters, romance, and wandering life into a tramp's tale of ships and shores.
31452-roy-blakeley-in-the-haunted-camp:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh's Roy Blakeley in the Haunted Camp was published by Grosset and Dunlap with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. It follows Roy Blakeley and his fellow scouts into a camp with a haunted reputation. Fitzhugh, author of the Tom Slade and Pee-Wee Harris books, illustrated here by R. Emmett Owen, builds the story around scout life: work, fun, and the rumors that grow up around a strange place.

The boys mingle fun with their work, as one illustration caption puts it, and the haunted camp gives their summer a mystery to solve. Written for young readers, the book teaches teamwork and courage through adventure rather than lecture. It is a cheerful entry in a long-running series that made scouting itself the hero of boys' fiction.
32045-the-boy-scouts-in-a-trapper-s-camp:
Thornton W. Burgess's boys' adventure story, published by the Penn Publishing Company in 1915 with drawings by F. A. Anderson, sends the Boy Scouts to a trapper's camp. Burgess, already known for The Boy Scouts of Woodcraft Camp and The Boy Scouts on Swift River, dedicated the book to W. H. T. and his three boys. Its contents promise winter camping, woodcraft, and trouble on the fur trails.

The chapters move from an interrupted dream and Pat's sight of white magic, through the Blue Tortoise Patrol, snow-shoes and fish, and life on the fur trails, to Christmas in Smugglers' Hollow. A deer yard, poachers, a silver fox, and a conference follow, with the camp of the poachers and the sale of a black fox near the close. Readers get a wholesome outdoor tale, where scouting skills, trapping lore, and fair play settle a conflict with poachers.
33382-penny-nichols-and-the-black-imp:
Joan Clark's Penny Nichols and the Black Imp, copyrighted in 1936, opens with a black imp, a mysterious package, and a threat, then follows Amy's trail behind a panel to a holdup. Its chapters move from an invitation to lunch and a bold move to a robbery, a studio, a visitor, and a missing workman. Clark writes for young readers who love a fast, girl-centered mystery.

Penny herself, sharp and brave, drives the tale, with clues that reward close attention. The book's pace is brisk, its Chicago setting vivid, and its villains suitably sly. For fans of series mysteries, Penny Nichols offers a lively, old-fashioned adventure, where a girl detective outwits grown-up crooks and saves the day.
33968-the-academy-boys-in-camp:
S. F. Spear wrote this boys' camp tale, published in London, Edinburgh, Dublin, and New York in 1909 by Thomas Nelson and Sons. Boys of Massillon Academy gather one June morning near term's end, and the roll-call opens a camp story. Chapters follow a costly yes, off for Whaleback, camp life, a swimming pool, a fog-storm, and a wreck.

Anemone Pool, a day of freedom, boys in a trap, an escape, missing boys, and a board on the Una carry the tale to tents down. Spear writes for boys who like camp, boats, and scrapes. The book remains a cheerful school camp story.
35034-lost-farm-camp:
Lost Farm Camp is a north-woods novel by Harry Herbert Knibbs. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York under a 1912 copyright. Harold James Cue drew the illustrations. Knibbs had written Overland Red. He dedicates the book to Gretchen, with a canoeing verse. Thirty-two chapters carry the Maine camp's year. Swickey shoots the bear in the first of them.

Old Avery hurries in from the woods, excited. A butter-stealing bear has raided the spring-hole crock again. His daughter Swickey watches her kitten Beelzebub torment a field-mouse. Trapping bears is against the law in August, Avery complains. Shooting deer is too, Swickey notes, yet they eat fresh meat. Avery's aim has lately tripled his front sights. The contents promise the camp's whole folk. Smoke finds employment, flees, and makes a last stand. Jim Cameron, Barney Axel, and Red Smeaton fill out the crew.
35123-the-ladies-book-of-etiquette-and-m:
The Ladies' Book of Etiquette, and Manual of Politeness is a handbook by Florence Hartley, printed at Boston by Cottrell. It was entered for copyright in 1860. The book calls itself a complete handbook for the use of the lady in polite society. Hartley also wrote a ladies' handbook of fancy and ornamental work.

The title page lists its range: full directions for correct manners, dress, deportment and conversation. It gives rules for the duties of hostess and guest at morning receptions, dinner companies, visiting, evening parties and balls. Useful receipts for the complexion and hair close it, with directions for the care of the wardrobe. In her opening, Hartley lays down a first rule: do unto others as you would have others do to you. No one who holds that rule, she says, can ever be truly rude.
35957-the-go-ahead-boys-in-the-island-ca:
The Go Ahead Boys in the Island Camp is a boys' adventure novel by Ross Kay. Kay wrote The Search for the Spy, The Air Scout, and other Go Ahead Boys books. Chapters open with making camp, then a mishap, then John hearing something in the night.

Sailing, drifting, and an unexpected meeting fill the early action. A predicament, danger, and a challenge carry the boys onward. An outcast figure enters at chapter thirteen, and George's strategy closes a later turn. Grant misses at a key moment, by a chapter's name. Readers get a brisk summer camp tale of boats, islands, and boy pluck from a prolific hand.
37554-the-bobbsey-twins-at-cedar-camp:
The Bobbsey Twins at Cedar Camp, by Laura Lee Hope, is a children tale. Grosset and Dunlap issued it at New York with rights in 1921. Flossie and Freddie watch men at a sawmill in the frontispiece plate. The twins series runs to many volumes, all listed up front here.

Chapters open with Freddie surprise and a spell locked up at home. Thanksgiving and Christmas trees lead the family off to Cedar Camp north. North woods fun, a nutting party, and sawmill play fill the middle. A sudden storm, snow, and a bare cupboard strand them in camp. A wildcat, snowball bullets, and a lost child search close it.
37800-girl-scouts-at-dandelion-camp:
Girl Scouts at Dandelion Camp is a girls' novel by Lillian Elizabeth Roy, copyrighted in 1921. Grosset and Dunlap published it at New York. Roy also wrote the Polly Brewster books. The first chapter names the troop the Dandelion Patrol. Juliet Lee exclaims at the old dandelions covering the lawn. The girls must pull a hundred roots a day. Ruth Bentley grumbles that ten new weeds spring for each one pulled.

Eighteen chapters carry the patrol into camp life. An unexpected proposition and an old campsite start the adventure. Ruth meets difficulties, and first lessons in scout work follow. A Fourth of July outing and a place called Bluebeard's Cave mark the middle. A capture and a reward for courage raise the stakes. New members join before the scouts meet John Dunstan at the close.
39569-the-adhesive-postage-stamp:
Patrick Chalmers, a fellow of the Royal Historical Society, argued in an 1886 London pamphlet that his father James Chalmers first thought of the sticky postage stamp. The Encyclopaedia Britannica had ruled in James Chalmers' favor, and the pamphlet prints that ruling: the claim that Pearson Hill put forth against it had not weakened the proof. Papers on the penny postage reform, left by the late Sir Henry Cole, stand with the case.

The preface says a writer of death notices can only repeat the standing view of a man's work, while the true sifting of claims falls to later hands. James Chalmers, a Dundee bookseller who died in 1853, had long pressed the post office for faster mails. The pamphlet keeps up a family and town claim against the fame of Sir Rowland Hill.
40179-the-carter-girls-week-end-camp:
The Carter Girls Week End Camp is girls tale by Nell Speed, out in nineteen eighteen. Speed wrote the Molly Brown and Tucker Twins sets in past years. A Burt house of New York brought this book out that year. Douglas Carter writes home to her dam from Greendale in part one. Her sire is on the mend, which floods the girls with joy and thanks.

Dr Wright told them last spring that his state was grave past hope. A long sea trip for him left the four girls home on their own. Their state was worse than the dam knew, the note owns at last. Eighty in the bank was near all their sire free cash then. They let out their fine home and camp to earn their keep in truth.
4116-christopher-columbus-and-the-new-wo:
Filson Young's complete biography of Christopher Columbus gathers the whole life, from the home in Genoa to the last voyage home in 1504. The road from Santa Fe to Huelva, walked with a sad heart and a small talking boy, opens the tale of hopes fallen to dust at La Rabida.

From there the narrative runs through first landfall, gold fever, conquest, chains at Cadiz, and final return. Young writes with sympathy and narrative sweep, never hiding the cost of discovery. Readers who want Columbus whole, in one long Victorian life, will find this the fullest single version.
41262-dan-carter-cub-scout-and-the-river:
Dan Carter, Cub Scout and the River Camp, by Mildred Wirt, bears a copyright of 1949. Wirt wrote many tales for young readers, and Dan Carter stars in a set of his own. The book opens on a summer river, in a sailboat that has lost its wind.

Dan complains that they will be late for the Cub Scout meeting in the Cave. Midge Holloway, a freckled boy of ten, drapes himself over the bow with his legs near the water. Midge's father, a Den Dad for Webster City Den Number Two, checks his watch by flashlight. The chapters ahead name a find in the sand, a coded message, and stolen furs. A warning to Dan and a missing code raise the stakes at camp.
42102-the-boy-scouts-mountain-camp:
Howard Payson wrote The Boy Scouts' Mountain Camp, copyrighted in 1912 in New York. Brinkerhoff drew four original illustrations. Rob Blake leads the Eagle Patrol at Hampton, and Merritt Crawford is his corporal. Things have stopped happening in Hampton, Rob laughs, ever since a schooner was blown up and Jack Curtiss lost his hoped fortune.

Two mysterious men and a midnight auto dash start the trouble. The scouts drift in a storm, camp in the mountains, and are captured. A thrilling escape, a forest monarch, and a buccaneer's cave follow. Trapped in a living tomb, Rob finds the heart of the mystery at last. Payson, a lieutenant, wrote many scout tales of woodcraft and pluck.
42490-outwitting-the-hun-my-escape-from-:
Pat O Brien of the Royal Flying Corps wrote Outwitting the Hun, his escape from a German prison camp. Harper and Brothers issued the book in New York and London in March nineteen hundred eighteen. The tale is inscribed to the North Star. Its light, he writes, marked his road to freedom.

Shot down in his last air fight, O Brien fell into German hands. An identity disk told his captors he was an American. The camp at Courtrai in Belgium held him till he leapt for liberty. Nine days in Luxembourg and a forged passport mark his slow crawl onward. Belgian homes hid him while German soldiers crossed his path. Holland at last set him free, and King George called him to meet.
4330-two-expeditions-into-the-interior-o:
Charles Sturt's complete account of his two expeditions into the interior of southern Australia joins both volumes in one text. The expeditions, made in 1828 to 1831, sought the sources of the inland rivers and recorded the soil, climate, and resources of New South Wales. Sturt's opening reflection on rivers frames the whole enterprise.

A river watched from its bank, he writes, shows only flood or drought, while its nature is learned at its source, among its feeders. The complete text lets readers follow both journeys without a break, from the first probes inland to the later surveys. It is the fullest form of a classic of Australian exploration.
47279-the-woodcraft-girls-at-camp:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy wrote The Woodcraft Girls at Camp, copyrighted in 1916 and published at New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Roy also wrote The Woodcraft Girls in the City and the Polly Brewster books. A frontispiece shows the girls watching a swallow's flight. The catalog dates the book to 1916.

Woodcraft, Ernest Thompson Seton's movement, taught wood lore through tribes, honors, and camp life. Roy's girls take the system to summer camp: tents, fires, trails, and the coup honors of the league. Girls' series books of the nineteen tens rushed to give their heroines the outdoors that boys' books had monopolized. Roy wrote dozens of such volumes. At Camp is the woodcraft summer in full: badges, songs, and one long holiday of competence.
47553-bobby-blake-on-a-plantation-or-los:
Frank A Warner wrote this boys' book, copyrighted in 1922, in his Bobby Blake series. Bobby is a schoolboy at Rockledge, fresh from a Thanksgiving football win over Belden. A sinking boat and a close call open the tale at school.

Then an unexpected vacation takes Bobby and his chums south to a plantation. The chapters promise a gale, a runaway horse, a land shark, and a scoundrel's trick. In the great swamp the boys face an alligator's jaws, a panther on their track, a moccasin snake, and a midnight prowler. A hunter's cabin and a great discovery close the run. Warner keeps the peril high and the pace fast.
49363-oakdale-boys-in-camp:
Morgan Scott wrote Oakdale Boys in Camp, with four illustrations by Martin Lewis. Scott also wrote Ben Stone at Oakdale, Boys of Oakdale Academy, and Rival Pitchers of Oakdale. A picture from page 132 tells the legend of Lovers' Leap, where Granger warns a friend that he seems inclined to take everything too literally.

The Oakdale boys trade school and diamond for tents, lakes, and campfire tales each summer. Scott fills the camp with fishing, pranks, a legend, and the small feuds of boy friendship. Such series taught boys to love the woods in print before they slept in them. Readers get clean, breezy camp adventure in the classic Oakdale line.
49972-pittsburgh-main-thoroughfares-and-:
Frederick Law Olmsted wrote a report on Pittsburgh main roads and the downtown core for the Pittsburgh Civic Commission. The group took up the plan in December nineteen hundred ten. The book came out in February nineteen hundred eleven. Photos show East Ohio Street, Fifth Avenue, and Liberty Avenue.

Olmsted counts miles of main roads in a ring round City Hall. Few streets, he finds, leave room to pass a tram and a cart at once. Wide trade has choked the core, the plates make plain. His fixes aim to meet needs now and years ahead. The gift page calls for a town that is useful and healthful. It asks for beauty too, in streets fit for work and rest.
50224-the-boy-scouts-at-mobilization-cam:
Boy Scouts at Mobilization Camp is a boys adventure novel by Robert Shaler, copyrighted in 1918. Shaler had written Boy Scouts of the Signal Corps and Pioneer Camp tales before. Contents open with good luck, a breakdown on the road, and rising suspicions. A hold up, an echo from the past, and a burning bridge raise the action.

Chapter one finds Hugh longing to visit the state camp where militia are mobilizing. Accusation, life in the mobilization camp, and the disappearance of Felix follow in the heads. Bud Morgan on the scent and a search squad drive the middle of the tale. War fever of 1918 gives this scout outing its topical ground and pace.
50588-the-fifteen-watt-tungsten-lamp:
The Fifteen Watt Tungsten Lamp is a master's thesis in electrical engineering by Clair Elmore Anderson. He took his bachelor's degree at the University of Illinois in 1911. The thesis was submitted in 1912 to the university's graduate school. Ernst Berg, head of the department, supervised the work.

Anderson describes the lamps he tested and the methods he used. Long sections give characteristic curves and spherical candle power measurements. The heart of the thesis studies overshooting, the brief flare of a new lamp, with theories and amounts worked out in curves. Conclusions close the study. The work shows early care in measuring the new tungsten lamps that were replacing carbon ones.
5100-alaeddin-and-the-enchanted-lamp:
John Payne's Alaeddin and the Enchanted Lamp retells the Arabian Nights tale in verse and prose, introduced by a letter and a poem of exile and return. Twelve years earlier, on a dreary winter day of drifting snows, Payne fled the mean miseries of workday existence, slander, and hate into the dreamland of the Orient distance under Syrian skies.

There he gathered the rainbow remnants of old glory lingering in ancestral climes, far from modern lovelessness. Alaeddin's lamp, ring, and princess follow in that spirit of recovered wonder. Readers get a Victorian translation that treats the Eastern tale as poetry, not mere adventure, and as an escape into story itself.
51425-the-autobiography-of-a-super-tramp:
William H Davies tells the story of his life on the road in a memoir reissued in New York in 1917. Davies was born in a public house kept by his grandfather, a retired sea captain proud of his small schooner. Chapters run from childhood through youth to his years of tramping in Britain and America.

Inside are berry picking, a canal boat, a house-boat, a lynching, jail, and the cattleman's office, told in plain order. Davies treats law in America, thieves, camps, and the ways a tramp makes a living along the way. The tale ends with success, as the tramp becomes a poet of note. Readers get a clear, unsparing life story, rich in the speech and habits of the road.
53803-report-of-a-special-committee-of-t:
A special committee of Halifax's city council reported in 1859 on improving the fire department and finding more water for fire purposes. James Barnes printed the report at Halifax, Nova Scotia. The committee explains its delays first: appointed right after the great conflagration of September 9, it was disorganized almost at once by changes among its members.

Halifax, a wooden garrison and port town, burned in pieces every generation, and water was its standing anxiety. The report weighs engines, companies, reservoirs, and the means of paying for them. Such pamphlets are the plumbing of civic history: unglamorous, exact, and the reason some streets survived to be old. The committee's care with its own excuses shows how slowly reform moved even with the ashes still warm.
53855-iberia-won-a-poem-descriptive-of-t:
Hughes wrote this long poem on the Peninsular War, Iberia Won, published at London in 1847; the head gives his initials only. The poem runs to many cantos, each followed by copious historical and illustrative notes nearly as long. Hughes had written an overland journey to Lisbon and revelations of Spain, and he revisited the battle grounds before writing. Impressions from those visits mix with the verse.

The war he sings is Britain's long fight in Spain and Portugal against Napoleon, the war of Wellington's rise. A poem on it, published thirty years after Waterloo, is a veteran-age act of memory. The notes carry names, dates, and anecdotes the verse cannot hold. Hughes writes as poet and tourist together, standing on the fields and rhyming what happened there.
54138-camp-cookery-how-to-live-in-camp:
Parloa, a lecturer on the science of cooking, wrote Camp Cookery: How to Live in Camp. Estes and Lauriat of Boston issued it under her copyright of 1878. She had written the Appledore Cook Book before this guide. The book speaks to parties who plan to rough it in tents for weeks at a time.

First come outfits and hints for comfort. A wall tent for seven or eight, a trench dug round it, and beds of boards and straw start the camp. Parloa praises a small sheet-iron box stove that packs into its own chest. Cooking chapters then give bills of fare and recipes suited to open air, few pans, and hungry campers. The aim is good food and sound sleep in the woods.
54406-the-religious-thought-of-the-greek:
Clifford Herschel Moore, professor of Latin at Harvard, wrote The Religious Thought of the Greeks, published by Harvard University Press in 1916. The book follows Greek religion from Homer to the triumph of Christianity. A first impression in November 1916 was followed by a second within a month.

Chapters open with Homer and Hesiod, who, in Herodotus's phrase, created the generations of the gods. Orphism, Pythagoreanism, and the mysteries come next, then religion in the poets and in fifth-century Athens. Plato and Aristotle get a chapter, and later philosophies another. Moore ends with oriental religions in the Roman West, Christianity, and the long contest between Christianity and paganism. Bibliographies and a specimen Roman calendar close the book.
54755-the-boy-scouts-of-woodcraft-camp:
The Boy Scouts of Woodcraft Camp is a scout novel by Thornton Burgess, issued at Philadelphia in 1922, with copyright in 1912. Corson drew the pictures, and Burgess dedicates the book to his wife. He had written other Boy Scouts tales of rivers and lost trails.

Twenty chapters open with the tenderfoot's arrival at camp. An initiation, a recall, and a specter in camp follow. First lessons and Lonesome Pond give the woodcraft heart. A shot in the dusk and a battle for honor raise the stakes. A poacher of Lonesome Pond and a haunted cabin close the action. Readers get a wholesome camp tale from the future author of Peter Rabbit.
55012-dred-a-tale-of-the-great-dismal-sw:
Dred, A Tale of the Great Dismal Swamp is a tale by Harriet Beecher Stowe, first out in eighteen fifty-six. Stowe was famed past the world for her past tale of a slave house. A verse on a man who flees to the great swamp heads the book. This print is of a late year past its first.

In her front note Stowe says she chose the slave states once more for two ends. As art, she says, no ground gives the tale man such play of light and shade, with two races locked in wild ties. Past art, the moral weight of the theme drew her most. The clash of free and slave grows more grave with each year of the lands life, she holds.
57-aladdin-and-the-magic-lamp:
A poor tailor's idle son meets a stranger who claims to be his uncle. This retelling of Aladdin and the Magic Lamp follows the boy into a hidden cave of treasure. The stranger is in truth a magician after one lamp.

Aladdin keeps the lamp and finds a genie who grants his wishes. Riches, a palace, and a princess follow, but the magician returns to steal the prize. Cleverness and the lamp's power decide the contest. The tale remains a classic of the Arabian Nights tradition. Later stage and screen versions kept the lamp, the genie, and the magician's trick in memory.
57081-the-memoirs-of-charles-h-cramp:
Augustus C Buell writes a shipbuilder's life in The Memoirs of Charles H Cramp, from J B Lippincott in 1906. Buell had written lives of Paul Jones and Andrew Jackson. The contents open with early shipbuilding in Philadelphia and the colonies, Joshua Humphreys, the embargo, and the rise of the packet lines.

Later chapters take up Cramp's own era: clipper ships in 1850, the armored ships and the Monitor, the American Steamship Company, and tours of British yards. Merchant marine bills, the Clyde lines, and the fight over navigation laws fill the policy chapters. American sea power is the theme.
57632-the-legend-of-the-lincoln-imp:
Kesson, signing as Ursus, wrote The Legend of the Lincoln Imp, at Lincoln. Ruddock printed the verse tale, first issued in 1904. Reprints ran on through 1944, the front pages list. A front plate shows the imp photographed in its actual place. That place is the Angel Choir of Lincoln Cathedral, the caption says.

The devil was in a good humour one day, the poem opens. He let out his sprightly young demons to play in the world. One dived in the sea and was not at all wet, it runs. One jumped in a furnace and got no scorch from the fire. One strode on the wind as on a steed to old Lindum. There'll be the devil to pay ere I leave it, he boasts. The imp vows to blow up chapter, dean, canons, and singers. Kesson gives the cathedral legend in comic verse.
59625-hemp:
Farmers' Bulletin number 1935 from the United States Department of Agriculture tells growers how to raise hemp for fiber. Robinson, a senior agronomist, wrote the guide, first issued at Washington in January 1943 and lightly revised in April 1952. Hemp fiber goes into twine and light cordage.

A stark note opens the guide. The hemp plant holds the drug marihuana, so growers had to sign up under the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937 and pay a fee of $1 each year. Later pages cover soils, seed, sowing, foes, and harvest. Most care goes to retting, the wet rot that frees the fiber, and to tests that show when the stalks are ready.
59705-the-island-camp:
Talbot wrote this story for the Sheldon Press at London. The Vaughan children, Robin, Peter, and Jan, wait out the day their Lennox cousins arrive. The island lies in the river at the bottom of the garden, a few minutes' pull across, left to the birds except in the holidays. A camp on it is the pleasure ahead, for the Lennoxes are Scouts like themselves.

Their mother, a jolly good mother for Scouts and Guides who never fusses, agrees to a night or two under canvas. One condition stands: Jan, who had pneumonia two years ago, shall not sleep out of doors. She sleeps in the gardener's cottage on the island, and is a camper by day. Robin, who camped with his troop last year, is to captain the rest. The book belongs to the open-air shelf, when scouting taught self-reliance and mothers were learning to allow it.
59904-tony-the-hero-or-a-brave-boy-s-adv:
Horatio Alger, Junior, wrote Tony, the Hero, a brave boy’s tale of life on the road. A L Burt issued the book in New York in eighteen hundred ninety. Alger had written Tom, the Bootblack and Joe’s Luck before. One plate shows Tony tying a downed tramp hand and foot.

A man and a boy climb a steep street as the tale opens. Rudolph the tramp dogs Tony’s path with plots from the first. A farm house, a set trap, and a night break in crowd in. Tony hires out as cook and house help to earn his keep. A face at the window and a duel of boys raise the heat. A fighting Quaker and a rich lady cross his road in turn. All ends well, the last chapter’s name promises in full. Short tales of Whitmarsh and a midnight ride pad the back.
61186-gramp:
Charles De Vet wrote Gramp, a science fiction story first printed in Worlds of If in May 1962. Its headnote warns: it is tough to see into minds when you are only a child, and tougher still when you see what scares you. The child telling the story can read the pictures in people's minds.

He asks Gramp why Gramma is making mad pictures at him: pictures like you are lazy, and like she wanted to hurt you. Gramp's eyes go wide, and he takes the boy for a walk down past the corn field, counting the holes his wooden leg makes in the gravel. Their secret word is abracadabra. De Vet writes the telepath child tenderly, through a grandfather's love.
62654-the-greycliff-girls-in-camp:
Harriet Pyne Grove wrote a tale for girls, issued in New York in 1923. Girls from Greycliff school pack for a camp in Maine with Patricia West, their English teacher. School shut in early June, and Merrymeeting Camp opens on July 5th, but a fine trip comes first.

The camp offers a tour to see Niagara, Toronto, Lake Ontario, the St Lawrence, Montreal, and the White Mountains. Hilary Lancaster waits at Cincinnati for Helen Paget and Evelyn Calvert, two girls from the South. Grove says the folk are made up, but the camp, its work, and some events come from real camp life.
62802-the-golden-boys-at-the-haunted-cam:
Wyman's The Golden Boys at the Haunted Camp was published in New York by Burt under a copyright of 1924. Wyman, dean of the Pennsylvania Military College, wrote the Golden Boys series for boys of twelve to sixteen. This volume stands eighth in its own list, after the electric cell, the fortress, the Maine woods, the lumber jacks, the river drive, radio, and the Allagash.

Chapter one, A Strange Proposal, opens at The Fortress just after taps. Bob and Jack Golden are called down to the telephone. Bob, passing the officer in charge and the aid with formal salutes, finds Rex on the line, sorry to pull him out of his cot so late. The frontispiece shows one of the boys stooping over a mark in the ground: Here's something, he cries.
63676-the-pluto-lamp:
The Pluto Lamp, by Stearns, ran in Planet Stories in the fall of 1954. The headnote calls it irony that the Commission of Galactic Astrography picked a prime misfit for a grand task. That misfit is Knucklebone Smith, chosen to light the lamp of Pluto.

Knucklebone was his real name, the tale insists, and he stood six feet eight while weighing no more than a hundred and sixty-five pounds. His face was long and horselike, and no one recalled a smile on it. Through a life of failed ventures he held fast to a faith in destiny. The Pluto Lamp itself was a relic of the first days of star flight, famed among spacemen. Freighters once went as far as Uranus and no farther, leaving Pluto dark.
66362-gloucestershire-friends-poems-from:
Harvey, a Gloucestershire soldier and poet, wrote these poems in a German prison camp. The book came out at London in 1917, and the catalog gives his initials only. His earlier book, A Gloucestershire Lad at Home and Abroad, had won warm praise. A bishop wrote that Harvey says what other English lads in Flanders want to say and cannot. This volume is dedicated to his mother, his best Gloucestershire friend.

Poem titles tell the camp's inner weather: Loneliness, Autumn in Prison, Prisoners, and Solitary Confinement. Christmas in Prison stands among them. Others reach home: English flowers in a foreign garden, a Christmas wish, and pieces for Kathleen. A commanding officer and a bishop frame the poems. They are plain, homesick, and brave.
66982-new-century-speaker-and-writer-bei:
Henry Davenport Northrop, a veteran maker of self-education books, compiled this standard work on composition and oratory for a Philadelphia publisher. It calls itself an unrivaled self-educator for young people. A galaxy of engravings brightens its pages.

The book teaches how to express written thought in a correct and elegant manner. Model selections from famous authors, subjects for compositions, and advice on description, pathos, and humor fill the first part. Then comes a peerless collection of readings and recitations, with programmes for special occasions, for schools, lodges, and Sunday-schools. Readers get the whole Victorian art of speaking well in one thick volume.
6738-the-four-canadian-highwaymen-or-the:
Edmund Collins bases his tale on fact, as his preface insists: everyone in that part of Canada who is not deaf has heard of the gang at Markham Swamp. Literary friends, he jokes, will call the book blood and thunder. They will say he is on his way to the dogs. Yet those same friends tempted the public with dull books and found no buyers. Collins will not quarrel with them.

The highwaymen themselves rob, ride, and hide in the swamp, in a story told with the gusto of a fireside yarn. Danger, pursuit, and rough justice drive the plot. The Four Canadian Highwaymen is a bold, old-style Canadian adventure, founded on a legend locals still told.
67787-the-rambler-club-s-winter-camp:
Sheppard wrote The Rambler Club's Winter Camp, published by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia in 1910. The author also wrote The Rambler Club Afloat and The Rambler Club in the Mountains. The book follows Bob Somers and his school friends on a winter trip into the woods.

The boys answer a fire-bell, form a bucket brigade, and then set off to build their camp. Chapters promise a first hunt, a skating match, a night alarm, and a wildcat on the trail. Later adventures include lost furs, wolves, a cave and a bear, and near-bandits. The story opens in Bob's cozy study at Pembroke Hall on a cold night, with algebra on his desk and snow outside. It is a hearty boys' adventure of its era.
67986-the-curlytops-in-the-woods-or-fun-:
Howard Garis, famed for his Uncle Wiggily tales, wrote this book for his Curlytops series. Cupples and Leon of New York published it in nineteen twenty-three, with art by Julia Greene. Ted and Janet Martin, the curly-haired brother and sister, leave home for a lumber camp in the woods.

Early fun brings a missing diamond, a lost crow, and their small brother Trouble with a squirrel. A hay wagon, a farmhouse attic, and a slide down a hill fill the trip with small thrills. At camp, Ted is caught in a scrape, and store and woods each hold a surprise. Garis writes warm, brisk tales for young readers, with a kind deed or a laugh on most pages.
68158-the-power-of-kindness-and-other-st:
Arthur, the temperance novelist who wrote Ten Nights in a Bar-Room, made this story book for the young. The Power of Kindness and Other Stories is a book for the example and encouragement of the young. Nelson published it at London in 1877. The first tale gives the book its name. Then come Ada and her pet fawn, how to avoid a quarrel, the broken doll, and harsh words and kind words.

A noble act, Emma Lee and her sixpence, the timely aid, and a story about a dog march on in order. The discontented shepherd and the wounded bird follow, each with its lesson worn openly. Nelson's books for the young filled Sunday school prizes across the empire. Arthur wrote to be understood by a child at one hearing. The lessons are kindness, honesty, and care for small things.
68214-the-old-paths-or-the-talmud-tested:
The Old Paths, or The Talmud Tested by Scripture, is a theological work by the Reverend Alexander McCaul, late professor of divinity at King's College, London. It was printed at London in 1880. Its full title promises a comparison of the principles and doctrines of modern Judaism with the religion of Moses and the prophets.

The advertisement to the second edition says nine years had elapsed since the work appeared as a volume. It had been translated into Hebrew, German, and French in the meantime. Its merits were discussed by the learned and unlearned of the Jewish people in all the countries of their dispersion. The reader is warned not to mistake the discussion of Rabbinism for an attack upon the Jewish people. To exhibit the Talmud in any European language, the author holds, is the most fatal attack that can be made on its authority.
68842-the-penultimate-trump:
The Penultimate Trump is a science fiction story by Ettinger, from Startling Stories of March nineteen forty eight. Its hero is Harley Haworth, a Wall Street battler now ninety two years old. Haworth's fortune is put at two billion dollars in greenbacked strength. His son is already an aged giver to good causes in the tale.

The old man fights his last war against death itself with failing strength. Doctors dose him with glands, vitamins, and transfusions of fresh blood. They cut out veins, an appendix, and one of his two kidneys. At last their shared wisdom shrinks to crackers and milk as a diet. Then the command changes: an engineer named Jones takes charge of the fight. Jones, called Garibaldi or Baldy, is a plain mechanical engineer by trade.
68975-the-crimp:
Henry Leverage wrote The Crimp, a sea story of the Barbary Coast of San Francisco. Its villain is the crimp, the boarding-house keeper who supplied sailors to ships, by fair means or foul. Captain Gully of the steam whaler Bowhead needs men, and the law for sailing masters, which protects seamen, blocks his way.

Cargoes rot in holds while wages for ordinary seamen mount beyond reach. The Bowhead lies ready for the Arctic whaling grounds with twelve men aboard, but Gully dares not sail without eighteen before the mast. He sends his mate Hansen to the Blubber Room on East Street for Abie Kelly, the crimp. Kelly comes at nightfall, drinks the captain's rum, and hears the order: six men before midnight, of any kind at all. Leverage builds a grim tale of the shanghai trade.
69137-the-unlit-lamp:
Radclyffe Hall published The Unlit Lamp with Cassell in 1924, her first novel. Hall had earlier written poems and a tale called The Forge. A line from Browning stands at the front: the sin charged to each frustrated ghost is the unlit lamp and the ungirt loin. Hall dedicated the book to Mabel Veronica Batten.

The novel runs to fifty chapters in five books, a long and patient telling. Its title points to a life that never gets lit: gifts unused, chances let pass, a self kept dim by duty and fear. Hall writes of a woman held fast in a narrow home and town, and of the escape that seems to offer itself too late. Readers meet the grave style she later made famous.
69909-cork-being-the-story-of-the-origin:
Cork, a short trade book from the Armstrong Cork Company of Pittsburgh, was printed in 1909. It tells where cork comes from, how it is made into goods, and what it is used for in the modern world. The firm wrote for general readers, not for experts, and backed the text with pictures. One early plate shows a great cork oak, called a monarch of the cork forest.

The story starts in the ancient world, where Greek and Roman writers already knew the cork tree. Cork had served for wine stoppers long before the time of Horace. The book then follows the bark from tree to factory and out into daily life. Its point is plain: after two thousand years, no cheaper stuff has yet pushed cork aside.
70237-the-unlit-lamp:
The Unlit Lamp is a tale by Elisabeth Sanxay Holding, the hand of past tales named on the title leaf. Its sub name calls it a study of the acts of folk on each past. It was put out at New York in nineteen twenty two. Its list of parts falls in three books and a tail piece. The first book bears the name of the bride.

A dance on an isle of the bay in eighteen ninety heads that book. A man of the tale in his home haunt, and that man at his court work, come next. The strange dame of the bride, and the bride as she learns to fit her self, fill the first run. The key note, a hedge that grew so fast, and a year past stand at its end.
71044-the-four-corners-in-camp:
The Four Corners in Camp is a girls' tale of a lake camp trip. Amy Blanchard wrote the set of books of the four young friends. It came out in the town of brotherly love in 1910. The four are Nan, Mary Lee, Jack, and Jean by name.

The tale starts with the four in a room in the chief town. A trip to a coast town and a kin dame fill the first parts. The start for camp and the climb up the hill come in their turn. Boats on the pond, a wet day, and a dawn dip fill the midst. A lad's bold deeds, a meal out, and a stage piece crowd the plot. A birth day feast and a straw ride lead to the close of camp. A bride's trip at the end sends the four home in joy.
7188-higher-lessons-in-english-a-work-on:
Alonzo Reed and Brainerd Kellogg built this schoolroom work on English grammar and composition around a visual method: sentence diagrams that lay out how words hang together. Their notes spell out the code. A heavy line marks the main clause, solid and dotted lines mark other links, and diagonal lines mark words set apart from the frame.

Pupils learn by drawing the shape of a sentence, so that subject, verb, and modifiers show their roles at a glance. The book joins grammar drill to composition, moving from parsing single sentences toward writing with care. Its plain, steady method made diagramming a familiar classroom tool, and this text preserves both the lessons and their drawn grammar.
72220-pee-wee-harris-in-camp:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote Pee-Wee Harris in Camp, copyrighted in 1922 and published by Grosset and Dunlap with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Barbour illustrated it. The catalog title keeps the closing words. Fitzhugh also wrote the Tom Slade and Roy Blakeley books, scouting's whole shelf.

The copyright page itself jokes: Pee-Wee Harris in camp, also in Dutch, also in hot water, in cold water, on the stage, in politics, and in the raspberry jam. It promises the true facts concerning his size, what there is of it, and his heroism, such as it is. Pee-Wee, the smallest scout and the largest appetite in the books, goes to camp at Temple Valley. A frontispiece shows him promising to close his eyes and try to go straight. Fitzhugh's comedy made scouting lovable to boys who never tied a knot.
73456-the-x-bar-x-boys-at-nugget-camp:
James Cody Ferris wrote this western story for boys, The X Bar X Boys at Nugget Camp, copyrighted in 1928 and issued by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. Walter Rogers drew the pictures. The X Bar X boys ride through a long series: on the ranch, at the round-up, and in Thunder Canyon.

A dangerous cast, a rescue out of the depths, and mysterious riders open this volume. An old miner and a girl with nerve, Belle Ada, join the cast at the gold camp of the title. Ferris wrote the West for boys in the plain series style of his house. The book is a clean, fast sample of the shelf.
73787-the-mysterious-tramp:
Vera Barclay wrote The Mysterious Tramp, published at London in 1920. She dedicated it to her cubby friends in the All Souls' Pack at Peterborough. Barclay also wrote Danny the Detective. The catalog title keeps only the last word. A frontispiece shows Black Bill leading a girl through a crowd to the big tent.

The contents open by firelight, then a council of war and the coming of Miss Prince. Danny the Detective gives a chapter its title. In the woods and the law of the Wolf Cub Pack follow, then a Wolf Cub council and the promise. The coming of the mysterious tramp arrives at chapter nine, with his story two chapters later. Barclay, a founder of the Wolf Cubs, writes scouting into adventure. Her tramp is the kind of mystery a pack can solve.
74525-the-bunnikins-bunnies-in-camp:
The Bunnikins-Bunnies in Camp is a tale for small young by Edith Davidson, with plates by Clara Atwood. It came out in September of nineteen nine. The book is writ with love to a small girl who loves those bun folk. Eight parts fill it, from the load of the ass to a fare well to the warm term.

The lead is a great dandy of a bun, with a fine white fur coat and the best of clothes past it. His hats, coats, ties, and gay socks are the toast of the young of his club. He weds a fair small bun, and two years on the pair take their two small ones to camp in the hills for his health. The small son is a bunch of strife who vows to be good for the trip.
76361-the-odyssey-of-a-torpedoed-tramp:
An officer signing himself only Y wrote these war letters, The Odyssey of a Torpedoed Tramp, published at London in 1918. Part one begins aboard the steamer Pamir off the coast of Morocco, August 22, 1914. Dear old thing, he writes home, you must be wondering what has become of me in this unholy mix-up. A month earlier they said goodbye in New Orleans, after a cakewalk at the Dollar Bar.

The Pamir loaded five thousand bales of cotton and hurried to clear for Liverpool and cooler weather. The news seemed inflammable, with headlines over Serbia, but the crew thought it a stunt of the press. A great sea-elephant nearly rammed them at the start. The letters follow the tramp steamer into a world at war, and to the torpedo of the title.
77636-sonnets-from-a-prison-camp:
Archibald Allan Bowman wrote Sonnets from a Prison Camp, issued in London in nineteen nineteen. John Lane published the poems in Britain and America. Bowman was an officer held in Germany. His proem is dated from the officers' camp at Hespe in August nineteen eighteen.

He who has never stood behind toothed wire, the proem begins, cannot know his theme. Freedom's wide room waits just past the fence, watched and helpless. Rastatt, an earlier camp, dates another poem to April of that year. In the Field, The Nadir, and On the March divide the set. Bowman turns a prisoner's shrunken days into strict sonnet form. Verse becomes his way past the wire.
77754-lefty-o-the-training-camp:
Burt Standish wrote this baseball novel, published in New York in 1914. Standish had already told of Lefty in the bush leagues, in the big league, and with the Blue Stockings. A front picture shows a manager gripping the young southpaw's hand and asking the usual questions.

Chapter titles sketch the plot: the grouch, the man with the queer eyes, and a manager's dilemma. A face in a mirror, doubtful denials, and a voice out of the darkness add mystery to the sport. Lefty must prove himself in spring training while someone works against him. Readers get the mix of baseball and intrigue that made Standish a boys' favorite for years.
79509-summer-camp:
Anne Herbert wrote Summer Camp, a pulp novel printed in New York by Softcover Library, and deposited in 1966. Its frame calls it a strange innocence. It began at the summer camp, when Peggy Matthews and Lilian Parker met in the counselors' cabin. After that, curiosity and desire had their way, the cover says, and Peggy had no idea what she was getting into.

A quoted doctor hails the book as an unforgettable story of an eighteen-year-old girl losing control of her emotions. Dozens of fresh-faced campers, eager young counselors, a nurse, and two earnest directors fill the swank girls' camp. The novel is a period piece of the paperback age, frank for its day.
79703-what-made-the-pinto-jump:
Ray Humphreys wrote a west tale of a pinto, a swindle, and a quick arrest. Humphreys also wrote Shorty's Squealers in the same vein. Marshal Pete Williams of Gunsight City tells his tale with pride. Sheriff Joe Cook and Shorty McKay hear him out in his room. A round from Monte Vista set the whole case in train.

A dude cowboy was sought for a bank swindle of eight hundred dollars. George DeNue came to town with a roll of cash soon after. The marshal jailed him and sent for the sheriff at once. A fat black cigar marks the sheriff's warm thanks for the work. West fans get brisk talk in full twang.
9195-the-slave-of-the-lamp:
Henry Seton Merriman wrote this romance of spies, love, and revolution, set first in a Paris street once called Rue de l'Empire. Chapters move from tools and burdens to reunions, broken threads, and puppets worked by hidden hands. A clue, a night watch, and a retreat lead to foul play and a stricken hero.

Christian Vellacott, true to his cloth, stands at the center as foes close in. Merriman keeps the intrigue taut and the feeling honest. The novel still reads as a brisk tale of secret work and open hearts in a Europe of plots.
9203-a-rill-from-the-town-pump:
Hawthorne gives voice to the town pump itself in this Twice-Told Tales sketch, set at Essex and Washington Streets in Salem. Noon by the north clock, noon by the east, and high noon by hot sunbeams: the pump declares its manifold duties, imposed in perpetuity. It claims to be town treasurer, guardian of the town's best treasure, water itself.

It chairs the overseers of the poor, giving bountifully to paupers without tax, and heads the fire department. The pump's comic boast carries a civic moral. The sketch remains a beloved Hawthorne fancy, witty, humane, and full of Salem color.
9648-tip-lewis-and-his-lamp:
Pansy, pen name of Isabella Alden, wrote Tip Lewis and His Lamp, a Sunday-school tale of a ragged boy's conversion. The tale opens in a crowded Sunday school, where scholars sing Happy Land and a teacher's seat stands empty. Half a dozen dirty, barefoot boys fill a long seat by the door, bright and cunning of face, bent on a frolic. Tip Lewis, their like, soon finds a lamp for his path.

The story follows Tip from mischief to faith, as teachers, hymns, and small kindnesses light his way. Pansy writes with warmth for poor children. A reader gets a beloved old moral tale, where a lamp stands for conscience, and a rough boy learns to shine.
a-drift-from-redwood-camp:
Bret Harte tells of a man Redwood Camp never valued: shiftless, worthless, carrying all he owned in a red handkerchief on a shovel handle. In a camp of strong men with sullen virtues and fascinating vices, he had neither, and no one even made him the camp's fool. He drifted out of camp on a plank in the great flood of 1856.

The short tale follows what the flood and the years made of this nobody, and how the camp's judgment of him came to look small. Harte builds the story on reversal: the least of the camp carries its moral weight. His Redwood Camp, among the giant trees, is the setting of his most famous fiction, and this piece shares its economy and sting.
a-rill-from-the-town-pump: Nathaniel Hawthorne gives voice to a Salem town pump in this short sketch from Twice-Told Tales, set at the corner of Essex and Washington Streets. Speaking through its nose at high noon, the pump claims every town office at once. It calls itself treasurer guarding the town's best treasure, head of the fire department, physician to the board of health, and keeper of the peace. Its boast is that water, freely given, outdoes tax-funded charity for the pauper.
aladdin-and-the-magic-lamp:
Aladdin and the Magic Lamp is a folk tale told here in plain form, credited to no known author. Aladdin, the idle son of a poor tailor named Mustapha, is approached by a stranger claiming to be his uncle. The man is in truth an African magician. He dresses the boy finely, wins the mother's trust, and leads him to a hidden place between two mountains outside the city.

There the magician opens the earth to a buried treasure vault that only Aladdin may enter. Sent down the steps, the boy finds the magic lamp whose keeper can grant him wealth and power. The tale follows his rise, his marriage to a princess, and the magician's attempts to steal the lamp back. It is among the best-known stories of the Arabian Nights tradition.
alaeddin-and-the-enchanted-lamp:
John Payne translated Alaeddin and the Enchanted Lamp from a recently discovered Arabic text, printing the volume in London in 1901. Payne dedicates it to Sir Richard Burton, his fellow labourer in the Thousand and One Nights. His introduction explains that M. Zotenberg found Arabic manuscripts in Paris containing the missing tales. Payne's conviction about Galland's interpolations stood confirmed.

Alaeddin, the tailor's idle son, is trapped by a magician in a cave of treasure. A lamp and a ring, each with its jinn, raise him to wealth and a princess. Zein Ul Asnam and the King of the Jinn, the companion tale, sends a prince hunting statues in dreams. Payne renders both in his ornate literal style, with dense notes. The book closed his great translation project as a final, disputed treasure.
britannica-1911-beauchamp:
Beauchamp names several weighty English families traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The baronial house of Beauchamp of Bedford was founded at the Conquest. Hugh de Beauchamp founded it and received a barony in Bedfordshire as his share. His eldest son Simon left a daughter as his heir.

Her husband Hugh was made earl of Bedford by Stephen in his reign. Yet the heir male, Miles de Beauchamp, held Bedford Castle against the king in 1137 and 1138. From his brother Payn came the later barons of Bedford in line. William held that castle against royal forces in the fight for the Great Charter. John fell at Evesham on the side of Simon de Montfort, and with him that line ended. A younger branch held a barony at Eaton Socon into the fourteenth century.
britannica-1911-crimp:
A crimp was an agent who supplied soldiers and sailors by kidnapping, drugging, decoying, or other illegal means. Such agents worked openly in the days of impressment. The word later covered anyone who supplied merchant seamen without a Board of Trade licence. It also covered the lodging-house keepers who preyed on sailors and often worked with crimps. The Merchant Shipping Act of 1894 set the legal line between lawful agents and crimps.

The act let port authorities licence and police sailors' lodging-houses and set penalties for abuse. It punished overcharging, the keeping back of seamen's effects, and soliciting. Officers could send a discharged seaman home and forward his wages for a small charge. The entry says these rules nearly killed crimping in the United Kingdom. In American ports, above all on the Pacific coast, state licensing and limits on blood-money cut the abuse down.
britannica-1911-damp:
Damp is a common Teutonic word for vapour or mist, kin to the German Dampf, steam, and so moisture in general. Its oldest sense lives on in the speech of coal-miners. Their firedamp is marsh gas, which, mixed with air and fired, leaves choke damp or after damp, carbon dioxide, behind. Black damp is a gathering of gases that will not support life or flame. White damp is sometimes used for carbon monoxide.

As a verb, damp means to stifle or check a movement. Damped vibrations are swings cut short instead of dying away on their own. The piano's dampers fall on the strings and stop their sound. A chimney damper, by narrowing the draught, slows the burning of a fire. One word thus runs from mine gas to music and the hearth. Each use keeps the core sense of something smothered or held down.
britannica-1911-gimp:
Gimp is a short word article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It gives two distinct meanings for one small word. The first is a stiff trimming used in dress and furnishing. The second is an old shortened form of wimple, a nun's throat cloth.

For the trimming, the entry explains how gimp is made. Silk or cotton thread is woven around a firm cord. A metal cord may run through it, and beads or bugles may cover it. Upholsterers used it to edge curtains, drapes, and chair seats. In lace work, gimp is the coarser thread that outlines the pattern and strengthens the cloth. The piece is a compact note for readers of old texts and craft terms.
britannica-1911-hemp:
Hemp is the bast fibre of Cannabis sativa, an annual herb. Its name matches Dutch hennep and German Hanf. Greek kannabis and Latin cannabis are cognate. Many unrelated plants unfortunately share the name hemp. Sunn hemp, Manila hemp and Sisal hemp are different plants. New Zealand flax is neither flax nor hemp. Deccan hemp comes from Hibiscus cannabinus. Pité hemp comes from the American aloe. Bowstring hemp comes from Sansevieria zeylanica.

The true plant is dioecious, like its relative the hop. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants. The female grows taller with darker foliage. She ripens five to six weeks later than the male. Males are pulled and steeped like flax when ripe. Females stand until the seed is perfectly ripe. Seed feeds cage birds and feeds oil mills. Fibre preparation, manufacture and trade fill long sections. Medical uses of cannabis close the account.
britannica-1911-imp:
Imp is a word whose sense has moved a long way over time. At first it meant a slip or shoot of a plant used for grafting. The verb was used for the grafting of fresh flight plumes on a hawk wing. Like the word scion, it then came to mean a child or heir of a great house.

The entry shows that shift with old quotes, one from Chaucer and one from a tomb stone. In time the phrase imp of Satan fixed the new sense. From then on an imp meant a small devil or a sprite that serves a witch. The piece is a short word study.
britannica-1911-shrimp:
Shrimp is a name for the smaller crustacea of the Macrura order, above all one food kind. A 1911 Britannica entry notes the common shrimp on north European coasts by its Latin name. Shrimp kin stand apart from lobsters and crayfish by their strong swimming limbs. Paddle like tail limbs drive them through the water with quick strokes.

The belly is most often sharply bent and looks humped when straightened out flat. The common kind thrives in shallow sandy water round the British Isles in plenty. It runs two or three inches long with a very short beak. Grey and brown speckles match the sand it lives on for safe cover.
britannica-1911-tramp: Tramp is a word for a vagrant who walks the roads from town to town. The brief 1911 Britannica note says such a man begs from house to house or claims to seek work. He has no home and sleeps out or in the casual ward of a workhouse. The word is a short form of tramper, one who walks with a heavy tread. Sailors also use tramp for a cargo steamer that runs no set line but picks up freight port by port.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-lamp:
The altar lamp burns continually before the tabernacle, commanded in the Old Testament as pure olive oil burning in the Tabernacle of the Testimony without the veil. The Church requires at least one lamp before the tabernacle. It serves as ornament, worship, mark of honour, reminder of Christ's presence, and profession of love. Mystically the light signifies Christ himself.

More lamps may burn before the Blessed Sacrament altar, always in uneven numbers: three, five, seven, or more. The lamp usually hangs by chain or rope before the tabernacle, high and clear of the altar steps, or from a side bracket within the sanctuary. Olive oil is prescribed as a symbol of purity, peace, and godliness, and leaving the Blessed Sacrament altar long without its light is a serious neglect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-kemp:
John Kemp was a fifteenth-century cardinal, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Chancellor of England, more statesman than bishop. Born at Wye in Kent about 1380 and educated at Merton College, Oxford, he practiced as a church lawyer so successfully that in 1415 he became dean of the Court of Arches. He also became vicar-general to the Archbishop of Canterbury. Henry V used him on embassies.

Made Bishop of Rochester in 1419, then of Chichester and London in quick succession, he joined the council after Henry's death. He backed Beaufort against Gloucester and became Chancellor and Archbishop of York in 1426. He led the fruitless Arras embassy of 1433 and was made cardinal in 1439. He put down the Kentish rebellion as chancellor again in 1450 and was transferred to Canterbury in 1452. He remained the king's mainstay against the Yorkists until his death in 1454.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-fecam:
John of Fecamp was an eleventh-century Benedictine abbot and ascetic writer, called Jeannelin for his small stature. Born near Ravenna early in the century, he studied at Dijon under his fellow-countryman William, Abbot of St. Benignus, mastering all the sciences and especially medicine, in which Bernier counts him among the cleverest products of the monastic schools.

Following William to reform Fecamp, John served as prior until 1028, when William made him abbot and retired to Italy. He defended his house's privileges and accepted the abbacy of Dijon in 1052. He resigned it in 1056 under the double burden, and late in life pilgrimaged to the Holy Land, where Turks imprisoned him until 1076. For the widowed Empress Agnes, who placed herself under his guidance, he composed ascetical works on prayer, contemplation, the heavenly Jerusalem, widowhood, virginity, and almsgiving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-dieka:
Wilhelm Diekamp was a German historian born at Geldern in 1854 and dying at Rome on Christmas Day 1885. Soon after his birth his parents moved to Münster in Westphalia, where he studied from 1867 to 1872, then theology at Würzburg and Münster from 1872 to 1875. Uncertain of his priestly calling, he abandoned it for philology, graduating doctor of philosophy in 1877 with a dissertation on Widukind, the Saxon leader, in history and legend.

Excessive study brought grave lung disease, which did not spare him effort. Teaching in public schools at Münster, Arnsberg, and Aachen while developing his historical training, he produced as evidence his Lives of St Ludger in 1881. That year the Westphalian Historical Association entrusted him with continuing the Westphalian Charter Book. In 1882 he became privatdozent, unsalaried lecturer, in history at Münster academy, after a year at Vienna studying diplomatics under Sickel.
christopher-columbus-and-the-new-world-o:
Filson Young's Christopher Columbus and the New World of His Discovery is presented whole in this Complete volume, the full 1906 life in one file. Young wrote from Spanish and Italian documents, advised on seamanship by Lord Dunraven. His four parts carry the Admiral from The Inner Light to Towards the Sunset. Genoa and La Rabida form the discoverer. Palos and the landfall make him immortal. Espanola's fevers unmake him. A Spanish deathbed closes the account.

Inside, Young keeps one standard: Columbus judged as a seaman and a man, not a statue. The gifts to Guacanagari, the lombard fired through the Santa Maria, Mendez's canoe, and the last pleading letters are all given in full narrative. Readers taking the biography whole get the standard popular life of its generation. It is warm to its hero's vision, honest about his government, and clear on what the voyages demanded.
doe-osti-17030335-report-summarizing-str:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-AMMT-031, by Wei-Ying Chen, Jiaxuan Li, Srinivas Mantri, and colleagues, studies how radiation changes a printed stainless steel. The steel, grade 316H, was built by laser powder bed fusion, a layer by layer printing method. Samples were hit with ion beams that mimic neutron damage, some while helium was added and some while under load.

Damage showed up mainly as void swelling, tiny cavities that grow inside the metal. As built and stress relieved samples swelled more than solution annealed and cold worked ones across most heat and dose ranges. Wrought 316H swelled less than the printed as built forms. The team also built a new rig for irradiating samples under steady pull.
doe-osti-2584762-monitoring-home-electri:
Prateek Shrestha and Kim Trenbath of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote technical report NREL/TP-5500-92393 in August 2025. The study monitors how homes use electricity, using secondary wireless meters rather than utility billing data. The devices, made by Copper Labs, pick up data broadcast by whole-home meters and relay it to a central server at minute resolution.

The analysis covers 17 homes in the Denver metro and Aspen regions of Colorado, paired with survey data on building features and equipment. Shrestha and Trenbath compare load patterns across homes with rooftop solar, electric versus gas heating, different occupant counts, and people working from home. Minute-level data reveals appliance cycles and brief usage spikes that hourly metering misses, pointing to peak load times and avoidable energy use.
doe-osti-3005957-assessment-of-deep-burn:
Argonne report ANL/NSE-25/37, dated July 31, 2025, asks how far once-through HALEU fuel can be pushed and what that does to fuel cost. E. Hoffman, A. M. Bachmann, and N. Stauff of Argonne wrote it with A. Cuadra and C. Lu of Brookhaven. The study contrasts fast and thermal reactors. In fast systems, a larger core and denser fuel can cut the enrichment a design needs. Burnup, size, and enrichment trade against each other in complex ways.

A literature review rates fuel and cladding options by readiness. Doped, large-grain uranium dioxide fuels such as Westinghouse's ADOPT are furthest along and already in commercial use. Mixed oxide fuel is mature abroad but still unlicensed in the United States. For cladding, chromium-coated zirconium alloys and HT9 steel lead the field. Cost tables in an appendix price transport and disposal routes for spent fuel and high-level waste.
doe-osti-3011002-characterization-of-tan:
A Tank 9H annulus sample was prepared and checked for Savannah River Mission Completion by Lawrence Oji and Hope Brown of the Savannah River lab. The work supports residual material inventory checks for the tank. Three vials reached the Shielded Cells in February 2025, each holding about 200 millilitres of annulus salt solution.

Each vial was filtered through 0.45 micron nylon membranes, and the filtrates were combined into about 600 millilitres of sample. Wet solids left on the filters totalled about 4.8 grams, drying to 2.1 grams after 72 hours in the cells. Ion chromatography found nitrate, nitrite, sulphate, phosphate, and oxalate above detection limits.
doe-osti-3022921-satellite-embedding-bas:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4420, by Byeonghwa Jeong, Daniel Adams, Andrew Zimmer, and Marie Urban, attacks a gap in global population mapping. The laboratory's LandScan program estimates population building by building, but footprint data are missing or sparse across much of the world, leaving those regions unmapped at fine resolution.

The proposed fix reads satellite imagery directly. Combining Google Earth Engine satellite embeddings with a UNet computer vision model, the framework imputes population on a grid without needing footprints. Applied to Taiwan as a test case, it reached an R-squared of 0.89 with a root mean square error of 18.70, beating traditional machine learning baselines. It also corrected false positives in settlement data, recognizing uninhabited places that building-based layers wrongly mark as populated.
doe-osti-3023470-differential-privacy-in:
Kaustav Bhattacharjee, Kapil Duwadi, Alex A Anderson, and Alka Singh of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory document a privacy upgrade to the Grid Kitchen software in March 2026. Grid Kitchen prepares power grid feeder models for sharing, but feeder data can expose sensitive operating details. Simple anonymization has failed in other fields when outside data let attackers re-identify records.

The team added differential privacy, which gives formal mathematical guarantees, inside the model dehydration pipeline. Carefully calibrated noise is applied to sensitive attributes under settings users can configure. Worked examples show a Laplace mechanism at epsilon 0.5 and a Gaussian mechanism with sigma near 0.969 in a moderate privacy mode, shifting a peak loading value to 73.05 percent. Modes trade protection against how much analytical value the shared model keeps.
doe-osti-3024392-hybridization-assessmen:
Soumyadeep Nag, Luis Fernando Enriquez-Contreras, Bikash Poudel, Trevor Atkinson, and Mahesh Acharya of Idaho National Laboratory, with Kyle DeSomber and Kevin Harris of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. They model a hybrid pumped storage design in INL/RPT-26-90192, dated September 2025. The system, called Trybrid, weds pumped hydro storage to batteries and solar generation, and the case study is the proposed Corral Summit plant.

This first part builds the power flow mathematics. Equations adjust battery power for conversion losses in each direction, direct current to alternating current and back, and set maximum charge and discharge currents after a loss adjustment factor. Open-circuit voltage and solar input enter the same bookkeeping. The point of the careful accounting is that a hybrid plant only delivers its promised flexibility if every conversion step is charged its real cost.
doe-osti-3025025-design-and-validation-o: Harsh environments got mechanically validated, and this DOE poster covers autonomous systems. The pages detail the design findings. The engineers get their data. The format was poster. The data were engineer. The autonomous were systems. The harsh were environments. The poster were format.
doe-osti-3362443-integrated-approach-to-:
F. Patrick McCluskey of the University of Maryland led this project under award DE-EE0009349, running from August 2021 to July 2025, with Sudip Mazumder and Arif Sarwat on the record. Solar plants fail most often in their supporting electronics, the inverters and module-level parts around the panels. The team built a non-destructive way to judge that gear health by fusing rich field data with machine learning, so owners can forecast failures before they cascade.

Synthetic datasets cut the bench testing needed to train those forecasts. Failure detective work fills much of the report: one case weighs over-voltage cratering, thermal runaway, and overcurrent as rival causes. Cross-sections cleared the wire bonds and die attach, while crater placement near the emitter bond pointed to overcurrent as the match.
doe-osti-3364305-final-technical-report-:
A final report from Auburn University closes DOE Early Career award DE-SC0021215, led by Bryan S. Beckingham in the Department of Chemical Engineering. The project studied how mixtures of dissolved species move through ion-containing polymer membranes. Such membranes sit at the heart of water treatment, fuel cells, and solar fuels devices, where they must pass wanted ions while holding back reaction products.

Single-solute movement was fairly well understood, but mixtures interact in tangled ways. The team synthesized membranes with varied ionic and neutral building blocks, then measured multi-solute diffusion with an in situ spectroscopic method that avoided older, laborious setups. Results tied membrane structure and water content to the mixture behavior that emerged. One applied study paired the membranes with a new catalyst and beat a commercial membrane's fuel cell performance.
doe-osti-3364916-resstock-measure-docume:
